The trio captures Paris in full autumn glory — warm amber and burnt-orange leaves, grey-toned Haussmann buildings, and that unmistakable sense that life is beautiful and worth chasing. Whether you work from home or run a busy studio, these prints remind you every single day why you do what you do.

The left print shows a charming Montmartre street café scene, with orange-striped awnings, flower-filled window boxes, autumn trees shedding golden leaves and a bicycle propped casually against the kerb. The centre print — inscribed with the handwritten phrase Paris aux couleurs de l'automne — shows a rooftop terrace overlooking the Eiffel Tower, dressed with dahlias in amber and orange tones, a bistro table set for two and plaid-draped chairs. The right print depicts a grand Gothic cathedral — Notredame-esque in character — surrounded by burnished golden trees and scattered autumn leaves in rich orange and yellow tones, all rendered in the same delicate watercolour palette of beige, grey and warm orange throughout the set.

How to Style motivational office wall art in Your Home Office or Studio

I'd hang all three prints in a clean horizontal row at eye level, with an even gap of about 4–6 cm between each one — that spacing lets each scene breathe while still reading as a cohesive set. The warm orange and beige tones work brilliantly against a soft white, warm greige or even a muted sage wall, so if you're thinking about a feature wall refresh, any of those shades will make the autumn colours really sing. Because the palette is earthy and restrained rather than bold, these prints suit both minimalist desks and fuller, layered home-office setups equally well.

If you've got a narrower wall or a gallery-shelf situation, try stacking them vertically — Montmartre café at the top, the Eiffel Tower terrace in the middle, cathedral at the bottom — and they tell a lovely visual story from street level up. They also work wonderfully in a creative studio, a therapy room or a small meeting space where you want the atmosphere to feel thoughtful and welcoming rather than corporate. Picking the Right Size and Finish for Your Wall

Before you choose your size, have a quick measure of the wall space you have in mind — it makes such a difference. As a general guide, for a standard desk-height office wall I'd suggest going for medium or large prints so the detail of those lovely watercolour scenes actually registers from sitting distance. Too small and you lose the charm of the Eiffel Tower peeking above the rooftops or the delicate leaf-scatter on the Montmartre street.

For finish, if your office gets a fair bit of natural light, Luster art paper is a great choice — it handles light beautifully without glare. If you want the absolute richest colour depth, Museum quality paper gives the artwork a gallery-grade feel that really does the watercolour palette justice. Motivational office wall art refers to art prints, canvas prints or framed artwork displayed in a workspace — home office, studio or commercial office — chosen specifically to inspire, energise or focus the person working there. Unlike purely decorative pieces, motivational office wall art is selected with intention: it might feature uplifting travel scenes that remind you of your goals, beautifully illustrated city prints that spark a sense of possibility, or calming imagery that keeps you grounded through a busy day. The right piece can genuinely shift the mood of a workspace, making it feel more personal, more creative and far more pleasant to spend time in. At AboutWallArt, our travel-style art prints — like this Paris autumn set — are a popular choice because they combine visual beauty with that quiet, daily reminder that life is full of wonderful things worth working towards.

How to Hang Motivational Office Wall Art as a Set of 3

1. Measure your wall space first: Hold a tape measure across the wall area you have in mind and note the width. For a set of 3 prints hung in a row, aim for a total span (including gaps) that sits comfortably within that space — roughly two-thirds of the wall width tends to look balanced rather than cramped or lost.

2. Mark your centre point: Find the horizontal centre of your wall section and mark it lightly with a pencil. Hang the middle print (the Eiffel Tower rooftop scene) centred on that point at eye level — approximately 145–150 cm from the floor to the centre of the print is a good general rule for a seated workspace.

3. Space the flanking prints evenly: Position the left print (Montmartre café) and right print (Gothic cathedral) with an even gap of around 4–6 cm on each side of the centre piece. Use a spirit level — even a free phone app works — to keep all three perfectly aligned horizontally.

4. Choose your fixing method: Framed and canvas-wrapped options come ready to hang. For framed prints, use two wall hooks per frame for extra stability. For unframed prints, use a frame or poster hanger you love — this set suits simple slim natural wood or matt black frames beautifully.

5. Step back and adjust: Once all three are up, stand back at desk distance (roughly 1.5–2 metres) and check the spacing looks even. Tiny adjustments make a big difference — take your time and enjoy the process!

aiItems.content:
What is fireplace wall art?

Fireplace wall art refers to art prints or canvases chosen specifically to hang above a mantelpiece or chimney breast, acting as a focal point for the whole room. Because the fireplace is already a natural centre of attention, the art placed above it tends to carry more visual weight than pieces hung elsewhere, so size, colour, and composition all matter a great deal. A set of prints — like a coordinated trio of travel scenes — works especially well in this spot because the grouped arrangement has the scale to hold its own above the mantel without requiring a single oversized piece. Choosing art that complements the tones of your fireplace surround and the wider room palette helps the whole space feel considered and intentional.

How to Hang Art Prints Above a Fireplace — a Simple Step-by-Step Guide

1. Measure your chimney breast: Note the full width of the wall space above your fireplace. Aim for your grouped prints to span around two-thirds to three-quarters of that width so they feel proportional — not cramped and not swamped by the wall.

2. Find the right height: The bottom edge of your artwork should sit roughly 15 to 20 cm above the mantel shelf. Any lower and the art risks heat or soot damage over time; any higher and it starts to feel disconnected from the fireplace below.

3. Mark your spacing: For a set of three prints, use a pencil and a spirit level to mark out the centre point of your wall, then work outward with equal gaps of 5 to 8 cm between each print. Cut paper templates to the exact print size and stick them temporarily to the wall with masking tape — this lets you step back and check the arrangement before you commit to any hooks.

4. Hang level: Use a spirit level across all three hooks or picture rails before hanging. Even a slight tilt will be very obvious on a fireplace wall because the horizontal line of the mantel acts as a natural reference point.

5. Step back and adjust: Once all three prints are up, step back to the opposite side of the room. Check that the grouping feels centred above the mantel and balanced in relation to any objects on the shelf below. Small adjustments now save a lot of fiddling later.

Unframed Print, Framed Print or Wrapped Canvas — Which Is Right for You?

Arrives ready to hang — Unframed print: No (you choose your own frame). Framed print: Yes, ready to hang straight away. Wrapped canvas: Yes, ready to hang straight away.

Paper / material — Unframed print: Luster art paper or Museum quality paper, your choice. Framed print: Luster art paper or Museum quality paper, your choice. Wrapped canvas: Canvas material, no paper choice needed.

Framing required — Unframed print: Yes — ideal if you have a favourite frame style or want to match existing décor. Framed print: No — frame is included. Wrapped canvas: No — no frame needed; the canvas wraps around a solid mount.

Best for — Unframed print: Maximum flexibility on frame colour and style; great if you already have frames. Framed print: Convenience and a neat, classic finish with no extra effort. Wrapped canvas: A relaxed, contemporary feel — especially suits the painted, illustrative quality of travel watercolour art.

Printed in the UK with fade-resistant pigment inks — Unframed print: Yes. Framed print: Yes. Wrapped canvas: Yes.

aiItems.content:
What is house wall art?

House wall art refers to decorative prints, canvases or framed artwork designed to be hung on the walls of your home, adding personality, colour and style to any room. It covers everything from travel-inspired watercolour art prints to botanical illustrations, abstract designs and typographic pieces. Good house wall art does more than fill an empty wall — it sets the mood of a room, sparks conversation and reflects the personality of the people who live there. Available as unframed prints, framed prints or wrapped canvases, house wall art can be tailored to suit any interior style, colour scheme or budget.

How to Hang a Set of 3 House Wall Art Prints

1. Measure your wall space first: Use a tape measure to find the total width of wall you have available. For a set of 3 prints, aim for the combined width of all three to fill around two-thirds of the wall — this creates a balanced, intentional look rather than prints that feel lost or crowded.

2. Find your centre point: Mark the centre of your wall lightly with a pencil. Hang the middle print first, centred on this mark at eye level (roughly 145–150 cm from the floor to the centre of the print). This anchors the arrangement.

3. Space the prints evenly: Hang the left and right prints with an equal gap between each one — 3 to 5 cm works well for most sets. Use a spirit level or a laser level to keep all three perfectly aligned horizontally.

4. Step back and check: Before making any final holes, hold the prints up with painter's tape or use paper templates cut to size. Step back across the room to check the spacing and height feel right from a distance — this is the view you'll have most often.

5. Choose your fixing method: For framed prints, standard picture hooks or adhesive strips work well on most walls. For wrapped canvases, a single D-ring hook per canvas is usually sufficient. Always check your wall type before fixing.

Choosing Your House Wall Art Print Format — What's the Difference?

Format — Unframed Print: The print only, ready for you to frame yourself or display as-is. Available in Luster art paper (slight sheen, vivid colour) or Museum quality paper (matte, gallery finish). Great if you already have a frame or want to choose your own.

Format — Framed Print: Your chosen art print comes ready mounted and framed — simply hang it straight on the wall. No need to source a frame separately. Available in Luster or Museum quality paper, in multiple sizes.

Format — Wrapped Canvas: The artwork is printed directly onto canvas and stretched over a wooden frame, with the image wrapping around the edges. Arrives ready to hang with no frame needed. Gives a contemporary, gallery-style finish. Available in multiple sizes.

Paper finish — Luster: A semi-gloss surface that brings out colour depth and fine detail — ideal if you want the watercolour tones in these Paris prints to really sing.

Paper finish — Museum quality: A smooth matte surface with a premium gallery feel — beautiful if you prefer a softer, more understated presentation with no surface reflection.

What is room art?

Room art is wall art chosen specifically to suit a particular space in your home — whether that's a hallway, living room, bedroom or kitchen — taking into account the room's size, colour palette, mood and how you use it day to day. A well-chosen piece of room art does more than fill an empty wall; it sets the tone for the whole space, adds personality and can even make a room feel larger or cosier depending on the style and scale you choose. At AboutWallArt we offer room art as individual prints or as curated sets — like this set of 3 — so you get a cohesive, gallery-ready look without having to match pieces yourself. Whether you prefer a travel scene, a botanical, or something abstract, the right room art brings the whole room together in a way that feels genuinely personal.

How to Hang Room Art in a Hallway: A Simple Step-by-Step Guide

1. Measure your wall first: Before you fall in love with a size, measure the width of the wall space you have available. For a set of 3, add together the widths of all three prints plus the gaps between them (allow 5–8 cm per gap). This tells you the total spread and stops any nasty surprises.

2. Find your eye level: The centre of your artwork should sit at roughly 145–150 cm from the floor — that's the standard gallery height and it works well in hallways where people are walking past rather than sitting down. Use a pencil to mark the centre point lightly.

3. Map out the positions before you put a nail in: Cut pieces of paper to the exact size of each print and stick them to the wall with masking tape. Step back and live with the layout for a day. This is the single most useful trick I know — it saves so many re-hanging headaches.

4. Use a spirit level: Even a small tilt is very noticeable in a hallway where you walk past every day. A small spirit level (or the level app on your phone) takes seconds and makes a huge difference to the finished look.

5. Choose your finish: Decide whether you'd like the prints unframed, framed (ready to hang straight from the box), or on wrapped canvas. Framed and canvas options come ready to hang, which is especially handy in a hallway where you just want to get it done and enjoy it.

Choosing Your Finish: Room Art Print Options Compared

Framed Print — Your print arrives already mounted and framed, ready to hang straight on the wall — no trips to the framing shop needed. A brilliant time-saver, especially for a set of 3. Available in multiple sizes on Luster or Museum quality paper.

Wrapped Canvas — The artwork is printed directly onto canvas and stretched over a wooden frame, giving a contemporary, frameless look with depth and texture. Arrives ready to hang. Available in a range of sizes.

aiItems.content:
What is minimalist art?

Minimalist art is a style that strips away the unnecessary and focuses on simple forms, limited colour palettes, and clean composition to create maximum visual impact with minimum fuss. Rooted in the 1960s art movement — with key figures such as Donald Judd, Dan Flavin, and Sol LeWitt — minimalism reacted against the emotional complexity of Abstract Expressionism by favouring order, repetition, and raw material honesty. In the home, minimalist art prints bring a calm, considered quality to a space, letting the viewer engage with shape, tone, and texture rather than narrative imagery. Today the term covers a wide range of abstract and geometric work, from stark black-and-white compositions to layered tonal studies like topographic or contour designs.

How to Hang a Set of 3 Minimalist Art Prints Above a Fireplace

1. Measure your wall first: Note the full width of your chimney breast or mantel wall. Aim for the combined width of your three prints to cover roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of that space — this keeps the set looking intentional and well-proportioned.

2. Find your centre point: Mark the midpoint of the wall. The middle print should be centred on this point. Work outward from there to position the left and right prints, keeping a consistent gap of 3–5 cm between each one.

3. Set the hanging height: The centre of the set should sit roughly 15–20 cm above the mantel shelf. This gives enough breathing room between the art and the fireplace surround and keeps everything at a comfortable eye level from across the room.

4. Use a spirit level: Even a small tilt will be obvious across three panels. Use a spirit level or a laser level to check all three prints are perfectly aligned before you fix them to the wall.

5. Step back and check: Once all three are up, step back to the opposite side of the room and look at the set as a whole. Small adjustments made now — before the hanging hardware is fully tightened — will save you time later.

What is an abstract painting?

An abstract painting is a work of visual art that uses shape, form, colour, line and texture to create a composition that does not attempt to represent the external world in a realistic or literal way. Rather than depicting recognisable subjects such as people, landscapes or objects, abstract painting communicates through purely visual elements — the arrangement of colour fields, gestural marks, geometric forms or flowing organic patterns. It is one of the most open and expressive movements in art history, rooted in the early twentieth century through artists such as Kandinsky and Mondrian but still very much alive in contemporary and decorative art today. In interior design, abstract painting prints are popular precisely because they work across so many styles and colour palettes — from minimalist and industrial spaces to warm mid-century rooms.

aiItems.content:
What is calming artwork?

Calming artwork is wall art designed to create a sense of quiet, peace and visual rest in a space — typically using gentle subjects like nature scenes, minimal landscapes or soft abstract forms paired with restrained, harmonious colour palettes. Rather than demanding attention, calming artwork works in the background of a room, giving your eye somewhere to settle and your mind a natural pause. It is particularly popular in offices and workspaces, where visual noise can add to mental fatigue, and in bedrooms or reading nooks where a relaxed atmosphere really counts. Styles like Japandi, zen landscape and ink-wash illustration are consistently among the most sought-after choices because they combine simplicity with real artistic warmth.

How to Choose and Hang Calming Artwork in a Home Office

1. Choose a subject that genuinely settles you: Think about what you find naturally peaceful — for many people that is open landscapes, trees, water or minimal nature scenes. This Japandi zen landscape set ticks all of those boxes with its ink-wash pine trees, still water reflections and soft misty background.

2. Keep the colour palette simple: Calming artwork works best when it does not compete with the rest of the room. A near-monochrome palette like the black, white and soft grey in this set — with just one quiet red accent — sits easily against most wall colours without adding visual clutter.

3. Hang at genuine eye level: Measure the centre of the artwork to sit roughly 145–150 cm from the floor — the point your eye naturally rests at when you look up from a desk. For a set of three, keep the gaps between panels even (around 3–5 cm usually looks best).

4. Give the prints some breathing room: Calming artwork needs space around it to do its job. Avoid hanging it between two very busy or colourful pieces — let it sit on a relatively clear stretch of wall so the minimal composition can actually feel minimal.

5. Pick the right finish for your light: In a bright office, Museum quality paper gives a crisp, gallery-flat look that suits ink-wash styles beautifully. In a lower-light space, Luster paper or a wrapped canvas can add warmth and depth.

Calming Artwork Options: Which Format Is Right for You?

Unframed Print (Luster or Museum quality paper) — The most flexible option. You choose your own frame or simply clip it to a board for a casual, relaxed look. Luster paper suits bright rooms with good natural light; Museum quality gives a flat, gallery-crisp finish that is ideal for showing off fine ink-wash detail. Best for: buyers who already have a frame in mind, or who like to swap art regularly.

Framed Print (Luster or Museum quality paper) — Arrives ready to hang straight out of the box — no frame-hunting required. A great choice if you want the set on your wall quickly and consistently presented. Best for: busy offices or anyone who wants a neat, finished look without the extra effort.

Wrapped Canvas — Printed directly onto canvas and stretched over a wooden frame, giving a painterly, textured quality that suits the traditional Japanese ink-wash style of this set particularly well. No glass, no glare, and the image wraps around the edges for a gallery feel. Best for: those who want depth and texture, or who prefer a more tactile, artistic finish over a flat print.

What is big living room wall art?

Big living room wall art refers to large-format art prints or sets of prints designed to fill and anchor the main walls of a living room — typically displayed above a sofa, fireplace or console table as the room's focal point. A set of three prints displayed side by side is one of the most popular formats because the combined width covers a large expanse of wall while the individual pieces remain easy to handle and hang. How to Hang Big Living Room Wall Art as a Set of Three

1. Measure your wall: Measure the width of the wall or the piece of furniture below (such as a sofa). Aim for the combined width of all three prints to span roughly two-thirds of that width for a balanced, intentional look.

2. Choose your size: Use the size guide images below to see how each print size looks in a real living room setting. When in doubt, go one size larger than you think — art that is too small tends to look lost on a big wall.

3. Mark the centre first: Find the centre point of your wall or sofa and mark it lightly with a pencil. Hang the middle print first, centred on that mark, then work outwards to the left and right prints.

4. Set your height: The centre of the prints should sit roughly at eye level — about 145 to 155 cm from the floor for most rooms. If hanging above a sofa, keep the bottom edge of the prints around 20 cm above the sofa back.

5. Keep gaps even: Space each print 5 to 8 cm apart. Cut a piece of card to that width and use it as a spacer while you hang — it keeps everything neat without any guesswork.

6. Step back and check: Once all three are up, step back to the opposite side of the room and look. Adjust any print that looks slightly higher or lower than its neighbours before the fixings are fully secured.

Unframed Print — The print only, ready for you to frame in whatever style suits your room. Great if you already have frames or want complete control over the final look. Available in Luster or Museum quality paper.

Framed Print — Arrives fully assembled and ready to hang straight out of the box — no sourcing a frame, no measuring, no hassle. The framing is already done for you, so you can hang it the same day it arrives. Available in Luster or Museum quality paper, in multiple sizes.

Wrapped Canvas — The artwork is printed and stretched over a wooden frame with the image wrapping around the edges for a clean, frameless contemporary look. Ready to hang immediately. Ideal if you want a modern gallery-wall feel with no frame at all.

Luster Paper — A semi-gloss finish that makes black ink tones crisp and vivid. Slightly reflective, which suits well-lit rooms beautifully.

Museum Quality Paper — A fine-art matte finish with exceptional colour depth and detail. No glare, a premium hand-feel, and the closest look to an original piece of artwork. Particularly well-suited to the Japandi and Zen aesthetic of these prints.

What is therapy office wall art?

Therapy office wall art refers to art prints and decorative pieces chosen specifically to create a calm, safe and welcoming atmosphere in a therapy, counselling or coaching space. The best pieces are visually open, non-threatening and emotionally neutral — they invite quiet reflection rather than strong reaction. This set of three Japandi-style ink brushstroke prints, with their minimal black, white and warm gold-toned palette, is a strong example: the imagery is abstract enough to avoid triggering associations yet meaningful enough to anchor the mood of a room. Thoughtfully chosen art in a therapy office can help clients feel grounded and at ease from the moment they arrive, which supports the work of therapy itself.

How to Choose and Hang Therapy Office Wall Art That Actually Helps Your Clients

1. Think about what your client sees first: Place art on the wall your client naturally faces when seated — not behind them. Art in the client's sightline contributes quietly to the feeling of safety and calm in the room.

2. Choose imagery that is open and non-prescriptive: Abstract or minimalist art — like these ink brushstroke prints — works best in therapy spaces because it does not lead the viewer to a specific emotion or memory. Avoid imagery with strong narrative or figurative content that could trigger associations.

3. Keep the palette calm and cohesive: Neutral tones — whites, blacks, warm earth tones and soft gold accents — create a sense of order and ease. A cohesive set of three prints, rather than mismatched individual pieces, helps the room feel intentional and settled.

4. Get the scale right: Measure your wall before you order. A set of three prints should span roughly two-thirds of the wall width for balanced visual weight. When in doubt, go slightly larger — art tends to look smaller on a wall than it does in a size guide.

5. Hang at eye level and space evenly: Aim for the centre of each print to sit at around 145–150 cm from the floor, with consistent gaps of 5–8 cm between each piece. Even spacing reads as calm and ordered — exactly the right message for a therapy environment.

Gold-toned accents in the art — All formats: the warm gold-toned scattered accents in this artwork are a printed colour tone — not real metallic or foil — and reproduce beautifully across all paper and canvas options.

What is oriental home decor?

Oriental home decor refers to interior design inspired by the aesthetics, traditions and natural motifs of East and South-East Asian cultures — particularly Japanese, Chinese and Korean design philosophy. It typically features a restrained colour palette, natural materials, clean lines and meaningful motifs such as blossoms, water, mountains and trees. The Japandi style — a popular modern blend of Japanese minimalism and Scandinavian simplicity — sits squarely within this tradition, favouring calm, balanced spaces over ornate decoration. At its heart, oriental home decor is about creating an atmosphere of peace and intentionality, where every object and artwork in a room earns its place.

How to Decorate with Oriental Home Decor: a Simple Step-by-Step

1. Choose a focal point: Start with one key wall — above a fireplace, behind a sofa or at the end of a hallway. Oriental and Japandi decor works best when you give it space to breathe, so pick one area to anchor rather than filling every wall.

2. Anchor with art: Hang your Japanese-inspired wall art prints first, as they set the colour palette and mood for everything else in the room. A monochrome set like this one in grey, black and white gives you enormous flexibility with surrounding tones.

3. Layer in natural textures: Add linen cushions, a bamboo tray, woven baskets or a ceramic vase. Oriental decor draws heavily on natural materials — these textures complement the artwork and reinforce the Japandi feel without adding clutter.

4. Keep furniture low and uncluttered: Low-profile furniture with clean lines suits the aesthetic perfectly. Avoid fussy ornaments; instead choose one or two considered objects — a smooth stone, a sprig of dried botanicals — and leave generous empty space around them.

5. Balance light carefully: Natural light is ideal for showing off the fine detail in monochrome Japanese landscape art. In the evenings, opt for warm, diffused lighting — paper lantern-style pendants or soft table lamps — rather than bright overhead lights, to keep the calming atmosphere intact.

No frame needed and no glass — gives a contemporary, gallery-style finish that suits the minimal Japandi aesthetic especially well. Available in multiple sizes.

Luster Art Paper — A semi-gloss finish that brings out the contrast between the deep black silhouettes and soft grey tones beautifully, with a gentle sheen. An excellent all-round choice for black-and-white artwork.

Museum Quality Paper — A premium fine-art finish with greater depth and detail resolution. Ideal if you want to appreciate every nuance of the reflected water texture and the moon's surface in this landscape set. The top choice for a statement piece above a fireplace.

What is an Asian Painting?

An asian painting is a broad term for artwork rooted in the visual traditions of Asia — particularly Japanese, Chinese, and Korean styles — characterised by subjects such as landscapes, nature, calligraphy, and scenes of daily life rendered with a sense of harmony and restraint. In a contemporary home-decor context, the term covers wall art prints inspired by these traditions, including Japandi-style pieces that blend Japanese minimalism with Scandinavian simplicity. Traditional Asian painting techniques often used ink wash, bold silhouetting, and negative space to evoke mood rather than detail — a quality that translates beautifully into modern print art. Today, asian painting wall art prints are popular choices for dining rooms, living rooms and hallways where a calm, grounded atmosphere is the goal. The style has evolved over centuries, absorbing influences from Chinese silk paintings and Japanese woodblock prints through to contemporary Japandi interior trends.

How to Hang Asian Painting Wall Art Prints as a Triptych

1. Measure your wall and furniture: Start by measuring the wall space or the piece of furniture beneath where you plan to hang the prints. Aim for the combined width of all three prints to be roughly two-thirds the width of the furniture below — this creates a visually balanced arrangement that feels intentional rather than accidental.

2. Mark the centre first: Find the centre point of your wall space and mark it lightly with a pencil. Work outward from that central mark so the triptych sits symmetrically. Hang the middle print first, then position the left and right prints with an even gap of 3–5 cm between each one.

3. Set the hanging height: The centre of your art arrangement should sit roughly at eye level — around 145–150 cm from the floor in most rooms. If you're hanging above a dining table, aim for the bottom edge of the prints to sit about 20–25 cm above the table surface, so the art feels connected to the space rather than floating too high.

4. Use a spirit level: Even a small tilt is very noticeable across three prints in a row. Use a spirit level or a level app on your phone to check each print is perfectly horizontal before you fix the hanging hardware in place.

5. Step back and adjust: Once all three are up, step back to the far side of the room and check the overall composition. Small adjustments in the spacing or height make a big difference — and with framed prints, you have a little wiggle room before committing.

Format — Unframed Print: The print is delivered rolled or flat, ready for you to frame yourself. Great if you already have frames or want to match a very specific frame style. Print only — no frame included.

Format — Framed Print: Arrives ready to hang straight out of the box — no extra shopping for frames needed. Clean, finished look with a protective front. Choose this if you want total convenience.

Format — Wrapped Canvas: The artwork is printed on canvas and wrapped around a wooden stretcher frame, with the image continuing around the edges. No frame required — gives a contemporary, gallery-style finish that suits Japandi interiors especially well.

Paper / Surface — Luster Art Paper: A semi-gloss surface that gives punchy contrast and a gentle sheen. Works beautifully with the reflective water and moon tones in this set.

Paper / Surface — Museum Quality Paper: A fine-art matte surface for a softer, more traditional gallery feel. Ideal if your dining room has strong natural light and you want to avoid any glare on the print.

Unframed Print — The print only, on your choice of Luster art paper or Museum quality paper. Best if you already have frames at home or want to choose your own framing to match your decor. Lightweight and easy to post.

How to Hang Office Wall Art for Men: A Simple Step-by-Step Guide

2. Lay the prints out on the floor: Before making any holes, arrange all three prints on the floor in front of the wall to check the spacing and composition. Decide whether you want them in a straight horizontal row or a slight stagger, and settle on the gap between each print — 5 to 8 cm is usually ideal.

3. Mark and hang the first (centre) print: Start with the middle print, hanging it at eye level (roughly 145–150 cm from floor to the centre of the print). Use a spirit level to make sure it's perfectly straight before fixing.

4. Work outwards to the left and right: Use your pre-measured gap to position and hang the left print, then the right, checking with a spirit level as you go. Step back frequently to check the alignment looks even from a distance.

5. Stand back and adjust: Once all three are up, step back to the other side of the room and have a proper look. Small adjustments now save regret later — it's worth taking an extra five minutes to get the spacing exactly right.

aiItems.content:
What are paintings in black?

Paintings in black are artworks that use black as the dominant or defining colour — either working almost entirely in black and white, or using deep charcoal and near-black tones as the foundation of the composition. They have a long and celebrated history, from the high-contrast dramatic works of Old Masters like Frans Hals through to the raw emotional power of abstract expressionists such as Franz Kline, whose bold black brushwork on white canvas became iconic. In contemporary home decor, black-led art prints are prized for their versatility: they work across a huge range of interior styles — from Japandi and minimalist to industrial and traditional — and their strong contrast means they hold the eye and anchor a wall with real confidence. Whether a detailed landscape, a silhouette, or an abstract composition, paintings in black bring a timeless, gallery-worthy quality to any room.

How to Hang Paintings in Black as a Triptych Above Your Fireplace

1. Measure your wall space first: Note the full width of your chimney breast or fireplace wall and aim for the combined width of your three prints to sit within roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of that width — this leaves comfortable breathing space on either side and stops the set feeling cramped or oversized.

2. Mark your centre point: Find the horizontal centre of your fireplace or mantelpiece and use a pencil mark on the wall directly above it. Your middle print should be centred on this point, with the left and right prints spaced evenly outward — a gap of around 3–5 cm between each print looks clean and intentional.

3. Set your hanging height: For above-fireplace placement, the bottom edge of the prints should typically sit around 15–20 cm above the mantelpiece shelf — close enough to feel connected to the fireplace, but with enough space that it doesn't feel cluttered.

4. Use a spirit level: Even a small tilt is very obvious with a three-print set, so take a minute to check each print is level before you fix the final hooks. A long spirit level laid across all three is the quickest way to get it right first time.

5. Step back and adjust: Once all three are up, stand at the far end of the room and check the arrangement from a distance — this is the view most people will see every day, and small adjustments at this stage make a big difference to the finished look.

Arrives ready to hang — Unframed print: No (you choose your own frame). Framed print: Yes, ready to hang straight away. Wrapped canvas: Yes, ready to hang straight away.

Flexibility to change the frame later — Unframed print: Full flexibility — pick any frame you like. Framed print: Frame included; swap it yourself if you want a different look. Wrapped canvas: No frame needed; borderless gallery look.

Ideal if you want — Unframed print: Full control over framing style and colour. Framed print: Convenience and a polished, finished look from day one. Wrapped canvas: A bold, contemporary statement with no frame at all.

A wall painting landscape is a printed art piece — or set of prints — depicting a natural outdoor scene, such as mountains, water, trees or sky, designed to hang on your wall as a decorative focal point. What are Asian Wall Art Panels?

Asian wall art panels are sets of two or more coordinated art prints inspired by East Asian artistic traditions — think Japanese landscapes, Chinese ink painting, and minimalist Japandi compositions. They are designed to be displayed together on the wall, either as a triptych or diptych, creating a single cohesive scene or a harmonious visual sequence. Popular subjects include moonrise landscapes, blossom branches, mountain scenery, and coastal waterscapes, often rendered in restrained palettes of black, white, charcoal, or soft neutrals. Displayed as a set, they bring a sense of calm, balance and considered style to any room — hallways in particular benefit from their ability to create visual depth and a striking first impression.

How to Hang Asian Wall Art Panels in a Hallway

1. Measure your wall space first: Before ordering, measure the width of the wall where you plan to hang the prints. Aim for the total combined width of the three prints — plus the gaps between them — to fill roughly two-thirds of that space. This keeps the arrangement feeling balanced rather than lost or cramped.

2. Find the right height: Hang the centre of the arrangement at eye level — approximately 145 to 150 cm from the floor to the mid-point of the prints. In a hallway this ensures the artwork is noticed immediately when someone walks in, without needing to look up or down.

3. Space the prints evenly: Mark your fixing points lightly with a pencil before you commit. A gap of 5 to 8 cm between each print keeps the triptych feeling connected without the prints touching. Use a spirit level — even a small phone app will do — so everything sits straight.

4. Step back and adjust: Once the first print is up, hold the remaining two in position before fixing them. Triptych arrangements can shift slightly once you're actually looking at the wall in context, so a quick check saves having to re-fix holes.

Modern art prints in this style draw on centuries of craft heritage — from Edo-period Japanese woodblocks to classical Chinese scroll painting — reinterpreted for contemporary interiors. Luster Art Paper — A semi-gloss surface that gives rich colour depth and a professional finish. Handles the deep blacks and bright whites of this charcoal landscape set with clarity. A great all-round choice.

content.productDescription:
Bring a genuine sense of calm to your workspace with this beautiful brown artwork set — three Japanese ink-style landscape prints that feel both deeply peaceful and quietly striking. Each print features flowing watercolour ink washes in warm brown and deep charcoal tones against a clean white ground, with softly painted silhouettes of a bonsai tree, a misty middle landscape, and a graceful arched bridge beneath a pale moon. Together they tell a story of stillness and nature that I think works perfectly in an office where you actually want to breathe and think clearly.

The Japandi style here is spot-on — that beautiful blend of Japanese wabi-sabi and Scandinavian simplicity that so many of us are drawn to right now. The rich, earthy brown ink spreads and pools in an organic, almost meditative way, while the charcoal-black silhouettes give real definition and depth. The white background keeps everything airy and uncluttered. Whether you love Asian-inspired art, oriental landscapes or just want something genuinely calming on your office wall, this set of three art prints delivers.

What's Included with Brown Artwork Japandi Japanese Ink Landscape Wall Art Prints | Set of 3

  • A set of 3 individual art prints, each featuring a distinct scene from the Japanese ink landscape composition
  • Printed in the UK using fade-resistant pigment inks for long-lasting, vivid colour
  • Suitable for indoor display — ideal for offices, home offices and calm, minimal spaces
  • Framed and canvas-wrapped options arrive ready to hang straight away, saving you the time and hassle of hunting for a frame that fits. The unframed option is the print only.
  • Choose between unframed and framed options in multiple sizes and in Luster or Museum quality; also available in wrapped canvas size options

How to Style brown artwork in Your Office or Home

I'd hang all three prints in a neat horizontal row at eye level, with an even gap between each one — around 5 to 8 cm works beautifully. Because the palette is grounded in warm brown, deep charcoal and clean white, these prints sit happily against off-white, warm grey, sage green or even a deep forest-green wall without any fuss. In an office, positioning them behind your desk or along the main wall you face creates that instant sense of calm focus — almost like having a Japanese garden in the room with you.

If you prefer a more layered look, try placing a low shelf or a simple wooden desk lamp beneath the set to carry the warm brown tones down into the room. The organic, painterly quality of the ink washes means they also work brilliantly alongside natural materials — think linen, light oak or rattan. For more Japandi styling ideas and complementary pieces, have a browse through our Japandi wall art collection — there are some gorgeous combinations in there.

Choosing the Right Size and Finish for Your Space

Before you decide on a size, it really is worth measuring your wall first — I always say that people tend to go too small rather than too large, and with a set of three prints the combined width can look really impressive when it fills the wall well. For a standard office or home-office wall, a medium or large size per print tends to give the most impact without overwhelming the space.

For finish, if you want the ink washes and fine silhouette detail to really sing, I'd lean towards Museum quality paper — it gives exceptional depth and sharpness. Luster paper is a brilliant all-rounder with a subtle sheen that reduces glare, which is especially handy in an office with overhead lighting. The wrapped canvas option is wonderful if you want a more contemporary, frameless feel that still looks completely finished on the wall.

Think about the mood you want the room to carry, too. These prints are genuinely calming — that warm, earthy brown and the quiet negative space do a lot of the heavy lifting. They won't clash or shout; they'll simply settle in and make the room feel more considered and serene. Scroll down to see how each size looks in an office before you decide — there is a size-guide image below showing every size in that room.

aiItems.content:
What is brown artwork?

Brown artwork refers to wall art prints and paintings where warm brown tones — from soft tawny beige through to deep rich chocolate — form the dominant colour palette. It is one of the most versatile and enduring choices for home and office interiors because brown is a grounding, natural colour that pairs easily with whites, creams, greens and neutrals. Brown artwork spans many styles, from abstract ink washes and Japandi landscapes to botanical prints and earthy abstract compositions. Choosing brown-toned art is a simple, effective way to bring warmth and a sense of calm to any room without the space feeling dark or heavy.

How to Choose and Hang Brown Artwork in Your Home or Office

1. Measure your wall first: Before you choose a size, measure the width of the wall or the space above your furniture. As a guide, the combined width of your art should fill around two-thirds to three-quarters of the wall width — this avoids the common mistake of going too small.

2. Pick a tone that complements your existing colours: Brown artwork spans a wide range — from light sandy tones to deep espresso. Look at your existing furniture, flooring and soft furnishings and decide whether you want the art to echo those warm tones (for a cocooning feel) or contrast them against a cooler wall colour for a bolder look.

3. Choose your finish for the light in the room: In rooms with strong overhead or natural light, a Luster paper finish reduces glare nicely. For offices or spaces where you want maximum depth and clarity in the print, Museum quality paper brings out the finest detail. A wrapped canvas works brilliantly in contemporary spaces where you want the art to feel sculpture-like on the wall.

4. Hang at eye level with consistent spacing: For a set of three prints, hang all three in a horizontal row with equal gaps between each frame — 5 to 8 cm is a reliable guide. Eye level is typically around 145 to 152 cm from the floor to the centre of the print. Use a spirit level or a long piece of string to keep the row straight before you put any nails in.

5. Style the space around the art: Once your prints are up, carry the brown tones into the room through small accessories — a wooden desk item, a ceramic pot or a linen cushion. This ties the artwork into the room so it feels intentional rather than an afterthought.

Comparing Your Options: Which Format is Right for This Brown Artwork Set?

Format — Unframed Print: You receive the art print only, ready for you to frame yourself. Ideal if you already have frames you love or want to source a specific frame to suit your existing décor. Available in Luster or Museum quality paper.

Format — Framed Print: The print arrives already mounted and framed, ready to hang straight from the box — no extra shopping required. A great choice if you want a polished, finished look without any effort. Available in Luster or Museum quality paper, in multiple sizes.

Format — Wrapped Canvas: The artwork is printed directly onto canvas and wrapped around a wooden stretcher frame, giving a contemporary gallery feel with no frame needed. Arrives ready to hang. Available in multiple sizes.

Paper Quality — Luster: A semi-gloss finish that gives rich colour with a subtle sheen. Reduces glare in brighter rooms, making it a practical choice for offices with overhead lighting.

Paper Quality — Museum: A premium fine-art paper with exceptional depth, sharpness and archival quality. Ideal if you want the finest possible reproduction of the ink wash detail and silhouette work in this set.
